q: Efficiency is a technical term that is derived from everyday usage.
e: The textbook explicitly states that efficiency is derived from everyday usage.

q: In physics and engineering, efficiency has a precise meaning.
e: Unlike everyday usage, efficiency has a precise, technical meaning in physics and engineering.

q: The term efficiency is used in association with machines and devices.
e: The textbook specifies that efficiency is associated with machines and devices.

q: A simple machine is a mechanical device that amplifies the magnitude of a force and changes its position.
e: This is the exact definition of a simple machine provided in the text.

q: Simple machines are used to make work easier.
e: The textbook states that the purpose of simple machines is to make work easier.

q: Nowadays, machines are just combinations or more complicated forms of the six simple machines.
e: Modern machines are described as combinations or complex forms of the six simple machines.

q: The six simple machines are lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, screw and wedge.
e: These are the exact six simple machines listed in the textbook.

q: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of effort to load.
e: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort ($MA = L / E$), not effort to load.

q: Mechanical advantage is defined as $MA = L / E$.
e: This is the correct formula for mechanical advantage as stated in the textbook.

q: In practice, friction is always present in a machine.
e: The textbook notes that friction is always present, meaning some effort is spent overcoming it.

q: Because of friction, the small effort applied will have to move through a big distance to lift a large load.
e: This is a direct consequence of friction and the conservation of energy in machines.

q: The ratio of the distance moved by the effort to that of the load in the same time is called the velocity ratio of the machine.
e: This is the exact definition of velocity ratio provided in the textbook.

q: Velocity ratio is defined as $VR = s_{\text{load}} / s_{\text{effort}}$.
e: Velocity ratio is defined as $VR = s_{\text{effort}} / s_{\text{load}}$, not the inverse.

q: The velocity ratio of a machine is usually much greater than 1.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the velocity ratio of a machine is usually much greater than 1.

q: In lifting a load with a machine, work done on the load is called the output work.
e: The work obtained by lifting the load is correctly defined as output work.

q: Work done by the effort during the same time interval is called the input work.
e: The work supplied by the effort is correctly defined as input work.

q: The ratio of output work to input work is defined as the efficiency of the machine.
e: This is the precise definition of efficiency for a machine.

q: Efficiency is generally expressed in the percentage form.
e: The textbook states that efficiency is generally expressed as a percentage.

q: Efficiency is related to MA and VR as $\text{efficiency} = (MA / VR) \times 100\%$.
e: This is the correct mathematical relationship between efficiency, mechanical advantage, and velocity ratio.

q: It is possible, in practice, to build a perfect machine for which output work is equal to input work.
e: It is impossible in practice to build a perfect machine; input work always exceeds output work due to friction.

q: Input work always exceeds output work.
e: Because some work is always lost to friction, input work must be greater than output work.

q: The efficiency of a machine must always be less than 100%.
e: Since input work always exceeds output work, efficiency can never reach 100%.

q: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the distance moved by the load to the distance moved by the effort.
e: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort ($L/E$). The ratio of distances relates to velocity ratio.
